key_cases.case_name: May v. Harrison County Department of Human Services
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's termination of a mother's parental rights, holding the clear-and-convincing burden had been satisfied and rejecting her argument that durable legal custody should have been ordered instead.
key_cases.relevance: Demonstrates how compliance with a court-supervised plan is measured against the statutory termination grounds at the next hearing.
key_cases.quote: The burden of proof in order to establish a case for termination of parental rights is clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.case_name: E.K. v. Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services
key_cases.holding: The Court vacated a youth court's neglect adjudication and rendered judgment for the child, holding the parents' notice and right-to-counsel protections were violated, the petition gave no notice of the circumstances alleged, and a parent's marijuana use without a causal connection to harm is legally insufficient proof of neglect.
key_cases.relevance: Court-ordered services imposed on the strength of a drug screen alone rest on an adjudication that cannot stand.
key_cases.quote: Elizabeth’s marijuana usage does not negate the requirement of a causal connection between the drug usage and the neglect.

key_cases.holding: Reviewing the statute de novo, the Court reversed a youth court's bypass of reunification, holding that Section 43-21-603(7)(c) requires both one of the three enumerated criteria and a best-interest finding, and that a father's pre-birth criminal history was not conduct to which he subjected the child.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Mississippi construction of when a youth court may order a disposition that dispenses with reasonable reunification efforts.
key_cases.quote: after determining that one of the first three criteria have been met, the youth court must also determine that bypassing reunification is in the best interests of the child

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the youth court's grant of durable legal custody of a chronically abused child to her long-time foster parents, but reversed the portion of the judgment permanently relieving the Department of Human Services of any further involvement, holding that durable legal custody leaves the parents' residual rights intact and ends only the mandatory annual dispositional reviews, not the youth court's jurisdiction or the Department's ability to monitor.
key_cases.relevance: Shows how a court-supervised permanency plan is converted into a disposition, and the four options - return to parent, relative placement, termination, durable legal custody - the agency and court must weigh.
key_cases.quote: The fact that under durable legal custody the parent retains some form of residual rights and responsibilities is a vital and obvious distinction to termination of parental rights.

key_cases.case_name: De La Oliva v. Lowndes County Department of Public Welfare
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed and rendered a judgment terminating a mother's parental rights and directed that custody of the child be restored to her, holding that the preponderance standard then prescribed by Section 93-15-109 was unconstitutional under Santosky v. Kramer and that the proof was in any event insufficient to establish abandonment or deep-seated antipathy by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: The welfare department had been ordered by an earlier chancery decree to file a plan for the child's return, never implemented one, and moved to terminate only after the mother sued for custody - the record of a service plan that existed on paper only.
key_cases.quote: The chancellor, in making her findings in the case sub judice, clearly relied on an unconstitutional and impermissible standard of proof.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed an educational-neglect adjudication, the ensuing neglect adjudication and a contempt citation and returned the child to her parents, holding that the Youth Court Act imposes a mandatory duty on the judge to advise the parties of their right to counsel and to explain the purpose of each adjudicatory hearing, and that noncompliance is reversible error.
key_cases.relevance: Disposition must follow a separate, distinct adjudicatory hearing, so service and placement orders entered after a blurred proceeding cannot stand.
key_cases.quote: The youth court did not inform I.G.'s mother and step-father of their right to counsel, as mandated by our legislature, and for this reason the cause must be reversed.
